Case Vignette: Mark

Mark is a 50-year-old married man, a clinical psychologist who has spent the better part of two decades helping others navigate their own traumas. He presents for therapy at the urging of his wife, Sarah, who has watched him become a stranger over the past nine months. He is precise in his language, analytical, and maintains a controlled, almost clinical demeanor during session, though his hands tremble slightly when he reaches for a glass of water.

The event that shattered his world occurred ten months ago. Mark was at a professional conference in a neighboring city. He met a colleague, a man he had known peripherally for years, at the hotel bar after the day’s workshops. They shared drinks and conversation, and Mark recalls feeling relaxed, even buoyant. He does not remember leaving the bar. The next thing he knows, he is in the colleague’s hotel room, disoriented, with the man on top of him. Mark froze. He describes it as a complete dissociation from his body—a silent, paralyzed observation from a corner of the ceiling. He did not fight. He did not scream. He simply waited for it to be over.

The morning after, Mark showered for forty-five minutes, dressed, and caught his flight home. He told no one. He told himself it was a meaningless, drunken encounter he had consented to but couldn’t remember. As a psychologist, he understood the concept of denial. He lived inside it.

In the weeks that followed, his world began to shrink. He stopped attending his weekly poker game with friends, claiming he was tired. He stopped running, his primary stress relief for two decades. He found he could no longer sit in his home office without his heart pounding against his ribs. The room, once a sanctuary of books and quiet reflection, now felt like a cage. He now works exclusively from his laptop at the kitchen table, facing the door, a position he justifies as “more practical.”

His clinical work has become a minefield. He has a client, a young man, who is processing a sexual assault. During their sessions, Mark finds his own throat closing. He feels a hot, prickling shame crawl up his neck. He has started to subtly redirect the conversation, offering cognitive reframes and behavioral strategies prematurely, avoiding the raw, embodied narrative his client needs to share. Last week, he found himself sweating through his shirt during a session, unable to speak, and ended the session fifteen minutes early, citing a migraine. He is terrified his professional competence is crumbling.

The most devastating symptom is his relationship with Sarah. He loves her, but he cannot bear her touch. A hand on his shoulder from behind makes him flinch. A casual hug in the kitchen makes him feel trapped, suffocated. He has not initiated sex since the assault. When Sarah reaches for him at night, he pretends to be asleep. He knows she is hurt, confused, and angry. He sees her crying in the bathroom, and he feels a profound, hollow guilt, but he cannot speak the words that would explain his withdrawal. The secret sits inside him like a stone.

He experiences intrusive images daily—the pattern of the hotel ceiling, the weight of the man’s body, the smell of expensive cologne mixed with alcohol. He wakes from nightmares gasping, drenched in sweat, but he cannot remember the dream, only the terror. He avoids the entire wing of his house where the master bedroom is, now sleeping on the couch in the den. He has become hypervigilant. In grocery stores, he scans for men who match his attacker’s build. He no longer goes to the gym, unable to tolerate the vulnerability of the locker room.

He is here, in this office, not because he wants to be, but because Sarah gave him an ultimatum. He is a man who has built a career on the architecture of the mind, and he is now trapped inside a crumbling structure of his own making, unable to find the door.
